content: Hepatica is a genus of herbaceous perennial plants that belong to the buttercup family, Ranunculaceae. These plants are native to central and northern Europe, Asia, and northeastern North America. Hepatica is sometimes referred to as liverleaf or liverwort, but it should not be confused with liverworts, which are also known as Hepaticae. Some botanists classify Hepatica within a broader interpretation of the genus Anemone, referring to it as Anemone hepatica. Between two and ten species of Hepatica are recognized, with some taxa often treated as varieties. These include: Hepatica nobilis (Common Hepatica) H. nobilis var. pyrenaica (H. pyrenaica): Found in the Pyrenees. H. nobilis var. japonica (H. japonica): Native to Japan. H. nobilis var. nobilis: Found in Europe, from the Alps to Scandinavia. H. nobilis var. pubescens (H. pubescens): Found in Japan. H. nobilis var. acuta (H. acutiloba): Known as Sharp-lobed Hepatica, native to North America. H. nobilis var. obtusa (H. americana): Known as Round-lobed Hepatica, native to North America. Hepatica transsilvanica: Found in the Carpathian Mountains and Transylvania. Hepatica cultivation has been popular in Japan since the 18th century (mid-Edo period), where varieties with double petals and diverse color patterns have been developed. These plants are noted for their ability to tolerate alkaline, limestone-derived soils and can grow in a wide range of conditions. They thrive in deeply shaded deciduous woodlands, particularly beech forests, as well as in scrub or grasslands exposed to full sunlight. Hepatica can grow in both sandy and clay-rich substrates, often in association with limestone. Moist soil and winter snowfall are essential for Hepatica's growth. While the plant is tolerant of winter snow cover, it is less resistant to dry frost. Hepatica typically grows to a height of 10 cm and produces hermaphroditic flowers from February to May. The leaves are basal, dark green, and leathery, with three distinct lobes. The flowers, which may be white, bluish-purple, or pink, are borne singly on hairy, mostly leafless stems. Pollinators such as butterflies, moths, bees, flies, and beetles are known to visit Hepatica flowers. The name Hepatica is derived from the plant's leaves, which resemble the three-lobed structure of the human liver (from the Greek word hepar, meaning liver). Historically, Hepatica was used as a medicinal herb. According to the doctrine of signatures, the plant was believed to be an effective treatment for liver disorders due to the resemblance of its leaves to the liver.
